steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both long chains of nucleotides, but they differ in chemistry, structure, and biological roles.

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an ‑OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an ‑OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
   → The extra hydroxyl in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
   • RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)

3. Strand architecture  
   • DNA: Typically double-stranded helix with complementary base pairing (A–T, C–G)  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded; can fold into complex 3-D shapes via intramolecular base pairing.

4. Length and permanence  
   • DNA: Very long, contains the entire hereditary blueprint; designed for long-term storage.  
   • RNA: Generally shorter (though some viral RNAs are long); acts as transient working copies or catalytic/structural molecules.

5. Biological roles  
   • DNA: Stores genetic information in the nucleus (or nucleoid in prokaryotes).  
   • RNA: Multiple functional types  
     – mRNA: copies DNA information for protein synthesis  
     – tRNA & rRNA: translation machinery  
     – snRNA, miRNA, siRNA, etc.: gene regulation, splicing, defense, catalysis (ribozymes)

6. Location  
   • DNA: Mostly nuclear in eukaryotes; also in mitochondria and chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions throughout cell (cytoplasm, ribosomes, spliceosomes, etc.).

7. Replication & turnover  
   • DNA: Replicates semi-conservatively once per cell cycle; proofreading yields very low mutation rates.  
   • RNA: Transcribed continually; higher error tolerance; rapidly degraded and replaced.

8. Stability  
   • DNA: More stable chemically and protected by histones; can last decades or longer.  
   • RNA: Susceptible to alkaline hydrolysis and RNases; typically short-lived.

9. Information vs. function  
   • DNA: Mainly informational.  
   • RNA: Both informational (mRNA) and functional (ribozymes, regulatory RNAs).

10. Evolutionary note  
   • Many scientists think life began with an “RNA world,” where RNA carried information and catalyzed reactions before DNA and proteins evolved.

In short, DNA is the long-term, double-stranded genetic archive, while RNA is the versatile, usually single-stranded molecule that reads, conveys, and actively uses that information in the cell.
